The Akali Dal was the major political party in Punjab. In 1973 it passed the 'Anandpur Sahib Resolution'. The following demands were made through this resolution:

1. Chandigarh should be made a part of Punjab.
2. The Punjabi speaking parts in other States should be included in the State of Punjab.
3. The recruitment of Sikhs in the Indian army should be increased.
4. More autonomy should be given to the State of Punjab.

The Akali Dal came to power in Punjab in 1977. While taking charge, it put forward some further demands along with these old ones, such as a larger share of river waters for Punjab and the status of a 'holy city' for Amritsar.

Trust between people is the basis of coexistence, and communalism destroys that trust. To put an end to communalism we should mix with people of different religions instead of staying apart from them. We should accept the good practices and the good ideas of each other. We should be able to look at our economic and social problems rationally and understand them, and we should not mix these questions with religion. When religious harmony is disturbed, we should search for the economic, political or historical reasons that are responsible for it, instead of blaming a religion. The chapter tells us that this is the only way to put an end to communalism and to strengthen national unity.

Regionalism thrives on regional imbalance in development. In the period after independence some States achieved more progress while some States remained backward. States like Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab and Tamil Nadu developed economically and industrially, whereas States like Odisha, Bihar and Assam remained undeveloped economically and industrially. The States that develop economically also progress in education, health and culture, while the backward States remain behind in education and civic amenities, and their people are harassed by problems of education, backwardness, unemployment and poverty. Such people begin to think that they are being cheated and kept away from the benefits of development, and the understanding between States is broken. Regionalism grows on both sides of this imbalance. The people of developed States begin to believe that they are superior because of their history and culture, look down upon the people of underdeveloped regions and are unwilling to share the benefits of development with them. The people of backward areas, in order to organise themselves, arouse their regional identity and try to glorify local traditions and culture unnecessarily to prove their uniqueness. In this way regionalism becomes strong, and it endangers national unity.

Communalism is a serious threat to the unity of our country, and it emerges out of narrow religious pride. The British sowed the seeds of communalism in our country, though people of different religions have lived together happily for many centuries. There is nothing wrong in being duly proud of one's own religion, but when this pride becomes excessive it turns into bigotry, and each one begins to consider his own religion superior and that of others inferior. This leads to religious fanaticism, which is the base of communalism and which makes a person oblivious of national interest. People of different religions then stop trusting each other, become suspicious of each other and look upon their own compatriots as enemies. Because of such thinking riots break out, hundreds of innocent people are killed, public property worth crores of rupees is damaged and public peace is destroyed.

Regionalism means having excessive pride about one's own region. It is one thing to introduce oneself as a Bengali or a Marathi person, but to think that one is superior to people of other provinces because of it is excessive regional pride. It is natural to feel love for one's province, but this love turns morbid when it becomes abnormal. Regionalism thrives on regional imbalance in development, because some States progressed after independence while others remained backward. It can affect developed as well as undeveloped States: the people of developed States begin to look down upon the people of backward regions, and the people of backward areas glorify their local traditions and culture unnecessarily to prove their uniqueness. Regionalism endangers national unity, and this evil can be tackled by reducing the imbalance in development.

In 1980 the movement for an 'Independent Khalistan' took root in Punjab and terrorist activities had begun during that period. Armed followers started gathering around the staunch Khalistan supporter Sant Jarnailsingh Bhindranwale, who was arrested in 1981 on the charge of the murder of the newspaper editor Lala Jagatnarayan, after which the situation worsened further. Because of these developments President's rule had to be imposed in Punjab in 1983. Bhindranwale went to stay at the religious place called Akal Takht, and his followers captured the Golden Temple and built a barricade of sand bags there, so that the area looked like a fort. This greatly disturbed the peace in Punjab and became a major challenge to Indian democracy. Therefore it became necessary to carry out 'Operation Blue Star' to get the terrorists out of the Golden Temple. The task was entrusted to Major General Kuldeep Singh Brar, and the operation began on the morning of 3rd June 1984 and ended on 6th June, with the Indian army functioning with great restraint.

Communalism is a serious threat to the unity of our country because it makes people of different religions distrust each other and look upon their own compatriots as enemies. Because of such thinking riots break out, hundreds of innocent people are killed, public property worth crores of rupees is damaged and public peace is destroyed. Due to the bitter memories of the riots people are estranged from each other and mutual trust receives a setback. Trust between people is the basis of coexistence, and if trust breaks, social unity receives a blow. National unity cannot be achieved without social unity. That is why it is necessary that we all counter religious communalism with all our strength.

MNF - Mizo National Front.
It was established by the Mizo leader Laldenga in 1961, and it demanded 'Greater Mizoram', an independent nation to be carved out of Tripura, Manipur and the Mizo majority areas of the Lushai hills.

NNC - Naga National Council.
It was established in 1946 by some educated Naga youth, and later, under the leadership of Angami Zapu Fizo, it made a demand for an independent State of Nagaland.

PLGA - People's Liberation Guerilla Army.
It was an organisation established by the Naxalites in order to maintain their influence in the areas to which their movement had spread.
